title: How Tech Works · Episode 4
chapters: How your phone camera takes a photo
Inside the battery in your pocket

units.t: How Tech Works. Episode four.
In this episode: How touchscreens feel your finger, How screens make pictures, How your phone camera takes a photo and Inside the battery in your pocket.
Part one. How touchscreens feel your finger.
Your phone screen has no buttons, yet it knows exactly where you tapped, swiped or pinched.
The secret is that your finger is part of an electrical circuit.
Press to connect.
Pick up your phone and tap an app.
The glass does not move or click, yet the phone responds instantly.

A touchscreen is really two things stacked together: a display that shows pictures, and a transparent sensor on top that works out where your fingers are, measuring tiny electrical changes many times a second.
The first touchscreens most people met were resistive, on early handheld organisers, GPS units, some ATMs and signature pads.
Two thin, flexible conductive layers sit separated by a tiny gap.
When you press, the top layer touches the bottom one, completing a circuit at that spot.
Resistive screens work with a fingernail, a gloved hand or a stylus.
But they need a firm press, feel spongy and traditionally handled one touch at a time.
Your finger as a conductor.
Almost every modern smartphone uses a capacitive screen.
Your body conducts electricity, mainly because it is full of salty water.
Beneath the glass sits a fine grid of transparent electrodes, usually made from indium tin oxide, which conducts electricity while letting light through.
The grid holds a small electric field.
When your fingertip comes close, it disturbs that field and changes the capacitance, the ability of nearby conductors to store electric charge, at the points nearest your finger.
You do not need to press at all; a light brush is enough.
That is why capacitive screens feel so responsive, and why they are covered by tough, smooth glass rather than soft plastic that has to bend.
Scanning the grid.
The electrodes are laid out in rows and columns, like lines on graph paper.
A controller chip rapidly tests each crossing, measuring how much its capacitance has shifted.
Where a finger rests, a cluster of crossings changes, and the chip calculates the cluster's centre.
Because each crossing is measured separately, the screen tracks several fingers at once.
This projected capacitance is what makes multi-touch gestures such as pinch to zoom possible.
The sensor only reports where fingers are; software decides what you meant.
It tells a tap from a long press by timing, a swipe from a scroll by speed, and a pinch by tracking two points.
Tablets use palm rejection to ignore your hand, and some phones add haptic feedback, a tiny vibration that fools your fingertip into feeling a click.
Gloves and raindrops.
Capacitive screens explain some everyday frustrations.
Ordinary woollen or leather gloves insulate your fingertip, so the screen cannot sense it.
That is why touchscreen gloves have conductive thread woven into the fingertips.
A standard plastic stylus does nothing for the same reason, so styluses for phones have conductive tips.
Water is the opposite problem.
Droplets on the glass conduct enough to disturb the field, so a wet screen may register phantom taps or ignore real ones.
Manufacturers use software to tell the small, steady signal of a raindrop from the moving signal of a finger, and some phones have a wet touch mode.
Even so, using your phone in heavy rain or underwater remains unreliable for most people.
From radar rooms to pockets.
Touchscreens are older than many people assume.
In the mid 1960s British engineer E. A. Johnson, at the Royal Radar Establishment in Malvern, described a capacitive touchscreen intended for air traffic control displays.
In the early 1970s engineers at CERN, the European physics laboratory near Geneva, built capacitive touchscreens to control a particle accelerator.
Resistive screens developed around the same era and spread through industry, kiosks and handheld gadgets.
The big leap into everyday life came in 2007, when Apple launched the first iPhone with a multi-touch capacitive screen designed for fingers rather than a stylus.
Within a few years, physical keyboards on phones had largely disappeared, and swiping had become something even toddlers attempt on picture books.
The key idea: A touchscreen is a transparent sensor over a display, and older resistive screens work when pressure pushes two conductive layers together.
Part two. How screens make pictures.
Everything on your screen, from a sunset photo to this sentence, is built from millions of tiny lights in just three colours.
Dots and three colours.
Look at a screen through a magnifying glass, or a drop of water, and the illusion falls apart.
The image is really a grid of tiny dots called pixels.
A 4K television has 3840 pixels across and 2160 down, more than eight million in all.
A modern phone packs in several hundred per inch, so the dots are invisible at normal distance.
Each pixel is usually made of three subpixels: red, green and blue.
Varying their brightness produces millions of colours.
Red and green together look yellow, all three at full strength look white, and all off look black.
This is additive mixing, the opposite of paint.
It works because the retina has three types of cone cells, and a screen simply stimulates them in the right proportions.
LCD: a light shutter.
Most monitors and many televisions use liquid crystal displays, or LCDs.
Behind the panel is a backlight, today usually LEDs, that shines white light the whole time.
In front are two polarising filters set at angles to each other, with a thin layer of liquid crystal between them.
Liquid crystals can flow like a liquid yet line up in order, like a crystal.
A small voltage twists or untwists them, changing how much light gets through the second filter.
Each subpixel has its own colour filter and tiny transistor.
The weakness is that the backlight stays on behind everything, so dark scenes can look slightly grey rather than truly black.
OLED: pixels that glow.
OLED stands for organic light-emitting diode.
There is no backlight.
Each subpixel is a thin sandwich of carbon-based materials that glow when current passes through.
To show black, a pixel simply turns off, giving deep blacks and strong contrast, and saving battery on phones when much of the screen is dark.
OLED panels can be thin and flexible, which makes folding phones possible.
The trade-offs are cost and ageing.
The organic materials slowly lose brightness, and blue ones fade fastest.
An image left on screen for very long periods, such as a news ticker or game scoreboard, can leave a faint permanent ghost called burn-in.
Manufacturers fight it with tricks such as subtly shifting the image.
Frames per second.
A screen never shows true motion.
It shows a rapid series of still images, like a flipbook.
The number of redraws each second is the refresh rate, measured in hertz.
Many screens refresh 60 times a second, while newer phones, gaming monitors and televisions reach 120 hertz or more, making scrolling and fast games feel smoother.
Films are traditionally shot at only 24 frames per second, so a screen often shows each movie frame more than once.
Some phones change their refresh rate on the fly, dropping as low as one hertz for a still image to save battery, then jumping back up as soon as you scroll.
The faster your finger moves, the more those extra frames matter.
Resolution and the eye.
More pixels are not always better.
Whether you can see the difference depends on pixel size, screen size and viewing distance.
The eye can only resolve detail down to a certain fineness, and once pixels are smaller than that at your distance, adding more brings little visible gain.
Apple built its 'Retina' marketing in 2010 around exactly this idea: pixels too small to pick out individually at a typical viewing distance.
It also explains why, for most people watching from the couch, an 8K television offers only a modest improvement over 4K.
Contrast, brightness, colour accuracy and how cleanly the screen handles fast motion often matter more to how good a picture actually looks.
The key idea: Every screen is a grid of pixels, each mixing red, green and blue light to make any colour.
Part three. How your phone camera takes a photo.
A phone camera's lens is smaller than a pea, yet it can rival cameras costing thousands of dollars.
The secret is less about glass and more about software.
Light in buckets.
A digital camera uses an image sensor, a silicon chip covered in millions of light-sensitive sites called photosites.
Each works like a bucket left out in the rain.
During an exposure, photons strike the silicon and knock electrons loose, and the photosite collects them.
Brighter light means more charge.
Afterwards the charge is measured and turned into a number.
Almost all phones use CMOS sensors, built like computer chips, which made them cheap and power-efficient.
A photosite counts light but cannot see colour.
Most sensors put a red, green or blue filter over each one, in a checkerboard patented by Kodak's Bryce Bayer in 1976, with twice as many green as red or blue.
Software estimates the two missing colours at each point from its neighbours, called demosaicing.
The small-sensor problem.
Phones are thin, so their sensors and lenses must be small.
A full-frame professional sensor is about 36 by 24 millimetres, and most phone sensors are a fraction of that area.
A smaller sensor gathers less light, so in a dim room each photosite may collect only a few photons.
Light arrives randomly, so with few photons the counts fluctuate from one photosite to the next, and the image fills with grainy speckles called noise.
The electronics add a little of their own.
This is a physical limit, not a manufacturing fault, and explains why phone photos once looked so poor indoors and at night.
Cramming in more megapixels can make it worse, because each photosite becomes smaller still.
Many photos in one.
The breakthrough was computational photography.
A modern phone is often already capturing frames before you press the shutter, and combines several into one picture.
Averaging many frames cancels much of the random noise, much as averaging many people's guesses cancels individual errors.
Combining shorter and longer exposures keeps detail in both a bright sky and dark shadows, a technique called high dynamic range, or HDR.
Night modes capture frames over a second or more and align them to correct for shaky hands.
All this happens in moments on dedicated processors.
The photo you see is not a single instant of light but a carefully assembled composite.
Software makes choices.
After merging frames, the phone keeps editing.
It adjusts white balance so a white shirt looks white under orange indoor light, sharpens edges, smooths skin and boosts colours to look pleasing.
Many phones recognise what is in the scene, such as food, faces or sky, and treat each part differently.
Portrait mode imitates the soft background blur of a large lens.
A tiny lens produces little natural blur, so software estimates how far away each part of the scene is, using two cameras, depth sensors or machine learning, then blurs the background artificially.
Look closely at hair or glasses edges and you can sometimes spot mistakes.
Different brands make different choices, which is why the same scene can look noticeably different on two phones.
Still a photograph.
All cameras interpret the world.
Film chemistry favoured some colours over others, and photographers have always chosen exposure and framing.
But phones push interpretation much further, and the line between capturing and creating has blurred.
Some features can erase unwanted people from the background, or combine the best expressions from several shots of a group.
A well-known controversy arose in 2023 over phone photos of the Moon.
A tester showed that one brand's processing added lunar detail missing from a deliberately blurred original, drawing on a model trained on what the Moon looks like.
Most processing is harmless and simply produces better pictures.
Still, a modern phone photo is best seen as the camera's best estimate of a scene, not a perfect copy.
The key idea: A camera sensor counts photons in millions of tiny photosites, and software later guesses the missing colours.
Part four. Inside the battery in your pocket.
Lithium-ion batteries power your phone, laptop, cordless drill and maybe your car.
Knowing how they work explains why they slowly fade, and how to make them last longer.
A tiny chemical shuttle.
Every time you unplug your phone, you carry a small chemical machine.
A lithium-ion battery has an anode, usually graphite, and a cathode made from a lithium compound with metals such as cobalt, nickel, manganese or iron.
Between them sit an electrolyte, which lets lithium ions pass, and a thin porous separator that stops the electrodes touching.
When the battery powers your phone, lithium ions travel through the electrolyte from anode to cathode.
Electrons take the long way round, through the phone's circuits.
That flow of electrons is the current doing useful work.
Charging pushes everything back the other way.
Why lithium.
Lithium is the lightest metal, and it is eager to give up an electron.
Together, those traits let a battery store plenty of energy without much weight.
Compared with older rechargeables such as nickel cadmium, lithium-ion batteries hold far more energy for their size and lose little charge sitting on a shelf.
They also avoid the memory effect that once led people to drain batteries fully before recharging.
That combination made truly portable electronics possible.
Australia has a direct stake in this story.
It is one of the world's largest miners of lithium, much of it dug from hard rock deposits in Western Australia and shipped overseas for processing.
A Nobel-winning invention.
In the 1970s, during the oil crisis, British chemist M. Stanley Whittingham built an early rechargeable lithium battery.
It used pure lithium metal and could be dangerous.
Around 1980, American physicist John Goodenough, working at Oxford, found a cobalt oxide cathode with much higher voltage.
In the mid 1980s, Japanese chemist Akira Yoshino swapped the reactive lithium metal for a carbon-based anode, creating a far safer design.
Sony sold the first commercial lithium-ion batteries in 1991, in a video camera.
The three scientists shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Goodenough was 97, the oldest person ever to receive a Nobel Prize.
Fading and charging smarter.
Your battery holds less charge after a couple of years because of chemistry, not a conspiracy.
Each cycle swells and shrinks the electrodes, and side reactions use up lithium.
A crust grows on the anode and traps lithium that can no longer carry charge.
Heat speeds this up, so a hot car dashboard in an Australian summer is especially bad.
Long periods at completely full or empty add stress.
Phones charge fast to about 80 percent, then slow down on purpose to avoid damage.
Partial top-ups are fine.
Keeping charge roughly between 20 and 80 percent helps, and optimised charging settings do this for you.
Use reputable chargers.
Cold only reduces performance temporarily.
Safety and disposal.
Lithium-ion batteries are generally very safe, but they pack a lot of energy and a flammable electrolyte.
If one is crushed, punctured, badly made or overcharged without protection, an internal short circuit can heat it.
That heat triggers more reactions in a spiral called thermal runaway, which can cause fire.
These fires are hard to put out and can reignite.
Warning signs are swelling, hissing, unusual heat or a strange smell.
Stop using and charging the device, and check your fire service's advice.
Crushed batteries cause fires in garbage trucks and recycling centres.
Keep them out of kerbside bins.
Use a drop-off point, such as the B-cycle scheme's supermarket and hardware store collection points, and tape the terminals first.
The key idea: A lithium-ion battery works by shuttling lithium ions between two electrodes while electrons do useful work through your device.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What makes a resistive touchscreen register a touch?
Answer. Pressing two conductive layers together.
Question two. How does a screen produce yellow?
Answer. It lights red and green subpixels together.
Question three. How does a phone sensor get colour information?
Answer. Filters over photosites, with software filling the gaps.
Question four. What happens inside the battery as it powers your phone?
Answer. Lithium ions move from the anode to the cathode while electrons travel through the circuits.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
